Stage 1 · Warm-up

Reading without all the words

Half the words in a message from a friend are missing. Nobody notices until they have to explain why.

💬✂️
1 · Somebody sends you this. What has been left out at the start?
The message

Been at the museum since eight. Nothing working. Don’t wait for me.

Choose one, then compare with a partner. Which word in the message told you?Choose one and tell your teacher which word in the message told you.Choose one and write down the word in the message that told you.

2 · Which of these do you leave out most often when you write quickly?

Work in pairs. Compare a real message each of you has sent today. Who leaves out more?Compare a real message you have sent today with your teacher. What did you leave out?Write out a real message you have sent today, then write it again in full sentences.

3 · Read the claim. How far do you agree?
A claim

“Leaving words out is not laziness and not bad English. It is a signal: it tells the reader that you two know each other well enough not to need them. Write in full sentences to a friend and you sound annoyed.”

Take a position and defend it in pairs. Your partner must find one case where you are wrong.Take a position and defend it. Your teacher will find a case where you are wrong.Write a paragraph defending your position, then name one case where it does not hold.

Written for this course. Messages between three museum volunteers, a note on a door, and an email.

1 · Read the explanation.
Two families of prefix

A prefix is a piece added to the front of a word that changes its meaning without changing its class. Legal and illegal are both adjectives; understand and misunderstand are both verbs. That is why prefixes are worth learning: once you know the piece, you can read a word you have never met.

The number family tells you how many: mono- one, bi- two, semi- half, multi- many, inter- between. The negative family tells you that something is not the case (il-, im-, ir-, in-, un-), is the opposite or a refusal (dis-), or has been done wrongly (mis-).

Choosing between the negatives
  • in- is the basic form, but it changes to fit the word: il- before l (illegal, illogical), im- before m and p (immature, impossible), ir- before r (irresponsible, irregular).
  • un- is the everyday alternative and attaches to almost anything: unhappy, unimaginative. Where both exist, they are rarely interchangeable: unable, not inable.
  • dis- reverses or refuses: disapprove is to think something is wrong, not to approve badly.
  • mis- is the only one that means wrongly: misunderstand, mishear, mislead.

The one that catches everybody

Biannual and biennial. Biannual is twice a year. Biennial is once every two years. They are opposites in frequency and differ by two letters, which is why careful writers avoid both and write twice a year or every two years instead.

And one more. Semi- does not always mean exactly half. Semi-retired is not half a career and semi-human is not fifty per cent of a person: the prefix means partly as often as it means half.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Two families, two jobs

The counting prefixes tell you a quantity and almost never change the rest of the word: mono- one, bi- two, semi- half or partly, multi- many, inter- between. They attach to nouns and adjectives alike: monolingual, bilateral, semi-detached, multi-storey, intercontinental. The negative prefixes do something different: they reverse the meaning of a word that already exists, and the word without the prefix has to be a real word. Irresponsible exists because responsible does; there is no irrable.

The in- family changes shape to fit the sound that follows: il- before l (illegal, illogical, illegible), im- before m and p (impossible, immature, impatient), ir- before r (irresponsible, irregular, irrelevant), and in- everywhere else (inconvenient, incapable, informal). This is not a spelling rule you can ignore: inlegal, inpossible and inresponsible are all errors.

Not the same kind of negative

un- is the everyday negative and attaches to a huge number of ordinary adjectives: unhappy, unimaginative, unmanageable. in- / il- / im- / ir- tend to sit on words of Latin origin and often feel more formal. Where both exist, they are rarely synonyms: unable is a plain lack of ability, incapable suggests a permanent one.

dis- is not simply not. It marks the opposite action or an active refusal: disagree is to hold the contrary view, disapprove is to judge something wrong, dislike is an active feeling — none of them means merely the absence of agreeing or liking. mis- means wrongly or badly and attaches to verbs: misunderstand, mishear, mislead, misjudge. Note that mistake and misery only look like members of the family; the prefix is not doing any work there.

Watch the traps. Bimonthly and biweekly are genuinely ambiguous in English — twice a month or every two months — which is why careful writers avoid them. Invaluable does not mean worthless; it means too valuable to measure. Inflammable does not mean fireproof; it means the same as flammable. And a hyphen appears mainly before a capital or a repeated vowel: multi-storey, semi-detached, pre-empt against multinational, semicircle.
